passages.happening:
The second lot comes out for the tribe of Simeon. The writer says at once where its land lay: ‘Their inheritance lay within the territory of Judah’ (verse 2).

He lists its towns in the far south, beginning with Beersheba (verses 2-8). And he explains the arrangement. “The inheritance of the Simeonites was taken from the territory of Judah, because the share for Judah’s descendants was too large for them. So the Simeonites received an inheritance within Judah’s portion” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Simeon is the only tribe that receives no territory with borders of its own. It gets a group of towns inside another tribe's land. The reason given is practical. Judah had more than it could use.

There is an older story behind it. Simeon and Levi, two of Jacob's sons, once took cruel revenge on the town of Shechem. On his deathbed Jacob said that their descendants would be scattered in Israel. In this book both are scattered, in different ways. Levi is spread through towns in every tribe, in God's service. Simeon is folded into Judah. Later lists of the tribes hardly treat Simeon as a separate tribe at all.

Judah's part should not be missed. Judah had been given the first and largest share. When it turned out to be more than Judah needed, part of it went to a brother tribe. The book does not say that Judah objected.

Beersheba, at the head of Simeon's list, was the well in the southern desert where Abraham and Isaac had both lived. It became the usual name for the southern end of the land.
passages.later:
Jacob's words are in Genesis: “I will disperse them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis 49:7).

The early church in Jerusalem dealt with its own goods in a way that recalls Judah's too-large share: “There were no needy ones among them, because those who owned lands or houses would sell their property, bring the proceeds from the sales” (Acts 4:34).
passages.asks: Judah had more than it needed, and a brother had nothing. Ask where your share is ‘too large’ for you: more room, more money, more time or more influence than you can use. Ask who the Simeon is that could live inside it. And ask whether you would let them, without making them feel it.

passages.happening:
Four more lots follow, for the tribes that settled the north.

The third lot is for Zebulun, with twelve towns (verses 10-16). The fourth is for Issachar, in and around the Valley of Jezreel, with sixteen towns (verses 17-23). The fifth is for Asher, along the coast toward Tyre and Sidon, with twenty-two towns (verses 24-31). The sixth is for Naphtali, in the hills west and north of the Sea of Chinnereth, with nineteen fortified towns, Hazor and Kedesh among them (verses 32-39).

Each account opens and closes the same way: the lot came out, and ‘This was the inheritance of the clans of the tribe’.
passages.hearers:
These four tribes received the region that later generations called Galilee: the Valley of Jezreel, the hills around Mount Tabor, and the country beside the lake.

The writer keeps to one pattern for each. A lot is named by its number. Borders or towns are given. A closing line says that this was the tribe's inheritance, clan by clan. The sameness is the point. No tribe is passed over, and each is treated in the same way, from Judah the largest to these smaller tribes far from the center.

Some of the towns have later stories. Shunem, in Issachar, is where a woman made room in her house for the prophet Elisha. Gath-hepher, in Zebulun, was the home of the prophet Jonah. The Bethlehem in verse 15 is a northern town of the same name, not the Bethlehem of Judah where David was born.

Asher's share reached toward the great trading cities of the coast, Tyre and Sidon. Those cities were never taken. The book of Judges says that the people of Asher lived among the Canaanites there.

To a first reader this was the far north, away from Jerusalem and the later centers of power. The prophet Isaiah, writing when armies had overrun it, called it a land in gloom, and promised that it would be the first to see light.
passages.later:
Isaiah's promise names two of these tribes: ‘In the past He humbled the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the future He will honor the Way of the Sea’ (Isaiah 9:1). “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2).

Matthew says where Jesus made his home and why it mattered: “Leaving Nazareth, He went and lived in Capernaum, which is by the sea in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali, to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah” (Matthew 4:13-14). Most of what the Gospels tell of his teaching and healing took place in the lands shared out in these verses.
passages.asks: The lands of Zebulun and Naphtali were far from the center, and for centuries nothing much was expected of them. Ask what place, or what people, you have written off as the edge of things. Ask whether you think of your own life that way. And remember where the light first shone.

passages.t: Dan, and a town for Joshua
passages.happening:
The seventh and last lot is for Dan. Its towns lay in the west, toward the coast across from Joppa (verses 40-46).

The writer adds a note about what came later. ‘when the territory of the Danites was lost to them, they went up and fought against Leshem, captured it, and put it to the sword’. They settled there and renamed the town Dan (verse 47).

Then, with every tribe provided for, the people turn to their leader. “When they had finished distributing the land into its territories, the Israelites gave Joshua son of Nun an inheritance among them, as the LORD had commanded. They gave him the city of Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, as he requested. He rebuilt the city and settled in it” (verses 49-50).

The section ends where it began in chapter 14, with the priest Eleazar, Joshua and the heads of the families at Shiloh, at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. “So they finished dividing up the land” (verse 51).
passages.hearers:
Dan's land lay beside the Philistines, and the tribe could not hold it. The note in verse 47 looks ahead to a story told in the book of Judges, when the Danites went to the far north and took a town there. That story is told in Judges 18. This note is one more sign that the book of Joshua was finished after Joshua's own day. The northern town of Dan later gave its name to a saying. ‘From Dan to Beersheba’ meant the whole land from top to bottom.

Then comes the detail that says most about Joshua. He receives his share last. He had led the nation for years. He had been one of only two faithful scouts. No one would have grudged him the first choice of the best land. He waits until every tribe and clan has its place, and then he asks for one town in the hills of his own tribe.

The town had to be rebuilt. Joshua's inheritance was something he still had to work on with his own hands, as he had told the people of Joseph to work on theirs.

Caleb's request opened the dividing of the land, in chapter 14, and Joshua's closes it. The two men who had trusted God when the rest of their generation would not are the two whose personal shares the book stops to record.

The final verse names once more who gave out the land and where: priest, leader and elders together, by lot, before the LORD. The long section is tied off as a single completed act.
passages.later:
Joshua was buried in the town he asked for: “And they buried him in the land of his inheritance, at Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim” (Joshua 24:30).

Jesus described leadership among his followers in the same shape: “whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all. For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:43-45).
passages.asks: Joshua took his share last, asked for one town, and built it himself. Ask where you have authority, at home, at work or in church, and whether you tend to take your portion first. Ask what it would look like to see that everyone under your care is settled before you look to yourself. And ask whether what you want for yourself is as modest as one town in the hills.
